nodes.label: Phase 1 Slice 4 Handoff
nodes.rationale: Ten tasks, twenty-five commits. Derivative bytes fell 92.5% on the same corpus slice 3 measured, and the L0 half matching slice 3's 7.3 MB to within its own rounding is the check that the two runs measure the same thing. Records thirty-one rulings, four briefed assertions that could not fail, and three cases where an implementer's own mutation found more than the briefed one.

nodes.label: Generated-File Freshness Is Not a Typecheck
nodes.rationale: tsc --noEmit was red for nine tasks and no gate noticed. The per-task bar ran eight Rust gates plus export-bindings, which regenerates and diffs the generated files — it proved BatchStatus.ts was current, which it was. Nothing in the bar compiled the TypeScript that consumes those bindings, and npm test passes regardless because vitest transpiles without typechecking. cargo deny and the web suite are permanently in the bar from here.

nodes.label: Cross-Tenant Scoping at the Query
nodes.rationale: Two findings, one a leak and one a write. An unscoped batch-status failure join leaked another library's part name; revision_source taking only a revision id let a derive job render onto another library's revision. Both raised by implementers who judged them out of scope and both overruled on placement for the same reason: a guard that lives away from the query it guards is the one that gets dropped.

nodes.label: CoreError::MalformedJobPayload
nodes.rationale: Its message told operators the row 'was not written by Lapidary'. But JobPayload::from_row exists precisely because an older Lapidary wrote rows a newer one must read, so version skew is the expected way to reach this error and the message pointed at the one cause that is not it. Fixed with a test that fails if the claim returns — nothing outside src/ pinned the wording, which is how it survived.

nodes.label: Re-Derivation Determinism
nodes.rationale: Two independent runs on separate volumes and separate databases wrote 7,501,328 bytes of L0 both times, and the on-demand L2 came out as the same BLAKE3 both times. Content addressing means a re-derivation is free of drift by construction — here it is observed rather than argued, which is what makes on-demand deriving safe.

nodes.label: Stale Progress on a Hidden Tab
nodes.rationale: react-query does not fire refetchInterval on a hidden document, so a user who starts a 10,000-part sweep and switches tabs returns to a progress line frozen at whatever the last poll saw. Nothing is lost and a reload shows the truth, but the page tells a stale story. index.tsx already reasons about the other half — not leaving a closed laptop asking about a completed scan forever — and this is the missing half.

nodes.label: Briefed Assertions That Could Not Fail
nodes.rationale: Four assertions would have passed against the bug they named, all in briefs rather than implementations: a migration-survival test whose 'pre-existing' rows were inserted after the migration ran; a byte-identity mutation that changed a recorded column and never reached the bytes; a fixture too coarse to drift; and a toggle assertion that passes in both worlds because an unknown toggle also renders unchecked.
